questions.question: How does closing a done channel broadcast cancellation, and who should close it?
questions.title: Done-channel broadcast and ownership
questions.direct_answer: Closing a done channel makes every current and future receive proceed immediately, so one close can broadcast cancellation to many goroutines. The coordinator that creates and owns the cancellation lifecycle should close it exactly once; workers normally receive from a <-chan struct{} and must not close it. Closing twice or sending on the closed channel panics, while a received value is irrelevant.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands close-as-broadcast, directional worker APIs, and single-owner lifecycle.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Closing done wakes every receiver, not just one.
Use chan struct{} because cancellation carries no payload.
The lifecycle owner closes done exactly once.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A done channel represents one lifecycle event: work is no longer needed. Closing it is useful because a receive from a closed channel can always proceed. Every worker selecting on `<-done` becomes eligible to exit, and workers that check later observe the same signal.

This differs from sending one value. One unbuffered send pairs with one receiver; it does not automatically notify an unknown number of workers. Closing creates the broadcast. `struct{}` is conventional because no data needs to travel—the event itself carries the meaning.

Ownership must be singular. The coordinator that creates the operation and decides it is finished closes done. Workers receive it as `<-chan struct{}`, which makes accidental sends or closes impossible through that parameter. Closing an already closed channel panics.

For example, main can launch three workers that wait on the same receive-only channel. After setup, main calls `close(done)`. All three record that they stopped, and a WaitGroup lets main wait for their return before checking the count.

A raw done channel is suitable for a small contained component with one clear owner. If several callers may request cancellation, I prefer `context.WithCancel`, whose CancelFunc is safe to call repeatedly and also composes deadlines and parent cancellation. In either form, cancellation is a request to stop; the owner still waits if it needs proof that cleanup finished.

sections.title: Close turns a receive into a permanent ready event
sections.content: A closed channel retains one durable state: no more values will be sent. Every receiver can observe that state without consuming it. This makes close a broadcast, provided one owner controls the transition.

sections.title: Concept guide · Done-channel broadcast and ownership
sections.content:
Cancellation signaling asks workers to stop. Closing a channel provides that signal because all blocked receives wake and later receives complete immediately. The value returned is the element type's zero value; with `struct{}`, there is no payload to misinterpret.

Channel direction documents roles. A coordinator keeps `chan struct{}` so it can close. A worker receives `<-chan struct{}` and selects on it alongside work or a blocked output send. The type system then prevents the worker from becoming a second cancellation owner through that reference.

Exactly-once close is essential. Two workers that both detect errors and both call close can race into a panic. Route error reports to one coordinator, guard a shared close behind `sync.Once`, or use a Context CancelFunc when multiple cancellation requests are legitimate. Do not recover from double close as normal control flow.

Signal is not acknowledgement. After close, a worker may still be finishing a non-interruptible operation or executing cleanup before returning. If shutdown must be complete, combine cancellation with WaitGroup, an error group, or a dedicated completion channel and wait for those tasks explicitly.

Also separate data-channel ownership. The sender that knows no more values will be produced closes the data channel. A consumer that stops early signals done rather than closing the producer's output. That division prevents send-after-close panics and gives every channel one understandable lifecycle.

sections.title: One owner broadcasts to many receivers
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  O[Coordinator owns done] -->|close once| D[done is closed]
  D --> W1[Worker 1 receive wakes]
  D --> W2[Worker 2 receive wakes]
  D --> W3[Future worker receive is ready]
  W1 --> C[Completion tracking]
  W2 --> C
  W3 --> C
```

questions.question: How does a done channel prevent goroutine leaks when a consumer stops early?
questions.title: Stopping blocked pipeline goroutines
questions.direct_answer: A producer can leak when it blocks sending after its consumer returns. Pass a receive-only done channel into the producer and select between the output send and <-done. The consumer or coordinator closes done when it abandons the stream, allowing the blocked producer to return. The producer still owns and closes its output channel, and completion should be awaited when shutdown matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can cancel a blocked send while preserving separate output-channel ownership.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A sender can leak when its consumer stops receiving.
Select between the output send and the cancellation receive.
The abandoning consumer or coordinator signals cancellation.
The producer owns and closes its output channel.
Wait for producer completion when cleanup must be finished.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A goroutine leak often begins with a normal blocking channel operation. A producer tries to send the next value, but the consumer has already returned. If no receiver will ever arrive, the producer stays blocked and retains its stack and referenced resources.

A done channel gives that send a second outcome. Instead of using `out <- value` alone, the producer selects between sending the value and receiving from done. When the consumer abandons the stream, it closes done, making the cancellation case ready and allowing the producer to return.

The two channel lifecycles stay separate. The producer is the sender on out, so it closes out when it stops. The coordinator owns done because it decides that downstream no longer needs results. The consumer must not close out; doing so could make an active producer panic on its next send.

For example, main reads three numbers from an unbuffered generator and then closes done. The generator may currently be attempting its fourth send, but its select can take the closed done case. It defers closing both its output and an acknowledgement channel before returning.

Cancellation must surround every operation that can remain blocked, including sends between pipeline stages. A buffer can absorb a known bounded set but is not a general leak fix. I test early consumer exit and wait for the producer's acknowledgement so the test proves the goroutine actually stopped.

sections.title: Every blocking edge needs an exit path
sections.content: Pipelines work while downstream keeps receiving. Early return breaks that assumption, so upstream sends need an alternative cancellation edge. Ownership then determines who closes the signal, who closes data, and who waits for completion.

sections.title: Concept guide · Stopping blocked pipeline goroutines
sections.content:
Start with an unbuffered output. Producer sends value one and consumer receives it, so both proceed. After a few values, consumer has enough information and returns. Producer reaches its next send, but no goroutine remains at the matching receive. That send can never finish.

Adding a done receive to the same select lets either event release the producer. Before cancellation, a ready consumer accepts the value. After close(done), the cancellation receive remains ready forever. If both are ready at once, select may choose either, so downstream should tolerate an already-in-flight value or stop receiving after it has signaled and awaited shutdown.

The producer defers close(out) because it knows when all sends have ended. A range consumer can then terminate normally. The cancellation owner closes done once because it knows the overall operation has been abandoned. These are different facts and therefore different channel owners.

For multi-stage pipelines, each stage selects on done while receiving upstream and sending downstream. One canceled operation can then propagate through every blocking boundary. A stage must still release files, network responses, or timers it owns; the signal only gives code a chance to run that cleanup.

Testing should force the early-exit path. Use an acknowledgement or WaitGroup with a bounded test timeout to prove producers return. Checking only that the consumer returned misses the leak. In request-oriented code, Context usually carries the same cancellation through the call tree, but the blocked-operation reasoning remains identical.

sections.title: Cancellation opens an escape from a blocked send
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Producer computes value] --> S{select}
  S -->|Consumer ready| O[Send on out]
  O --> P
  S -->|done closed| R[Producer returns]
  R --> C[Producer closes out]
  X[Consumer exits early] -->|close done| S
```

questions.question: When should you use context cancellation instead of a custom done channel?
questions.title: Context cancellation versus a done channel
questions.direct_answer: Use context.Context across request, RPC, database, and API boundaries where cancellation must propagate with a deadline and reason through a call tree. Use a custom done channel for a small contained component with one simple lifecycle signal. Pass Context explicitly as the first parameter, call the returned CancelFunc to release resources, and let workers receive from ctx.Done rather than cancel their parent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can choose Context for propagated request lifecycles and raw channels for contained signaling.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Context carries cancellation, deadline, cause, and request-scoped values.
Derived cancellation propagates from parent to children.
Call the returned CancelFunc even when a timeout might fire later.
Pass Context explicitly as the first function parameter.
Use a raw done channel only when its local ownership is clearer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`context.Context` standardizes cancellation across API boundaries. It carries a Done channel, a deadline when present, an error or cause after cancellation, and carefully scoped request values. A derived context forms part of a tree, so canceling a parent cancels its descendants.

I use it for HTTP requests, RPCs, database calls, and work that should stop when the caller goes away. The function accepts context as its first parameter and passes it down. A worker selects on `ctx.Done()` alongside its blocking work and returns `ctx.Err()` or an appropriate domain error.

`context.WithCancel`, `WithTimeout`, and related functions return both a child context and a CancelFunc. The caller should invoke that function when work finishes, commonly with defer, because it releases resources even if a deadline would eventually cancel the context anyway.

A custom done channel is still clear for a private pipeline or component whose only signal is one owner saying stop. It avoids pretending the operation has request metadata or a deadline. Once cancellation crosses packages or needs composition, Context is usually the familiar contract.

For example, main creates a cancelable context, starts a worker, calls cancel, and receives `context.Canceled` from a buffered result channel. Cancel does not wait for the worker; the result receive provides completion. I do not store Context in a struct for ordinary APIs or let a callee replace its parent's cancellation authority.

sections.title: Context is a propagated lifecycle contract
sections.content: A raw channel communicates one event. Context builds a tree of that event plus deadline, error, and request-scoped values using a standard interface understood by the library ecosystem. Choose the smallest contract that matches the boundary.

sections.title: Concept guide · Context cancellation versus a done channel
sections.content:
A caller derives a child context from its own parent. The child Done channel closes when the caller invokes cancel, when its deadline expires, or when the parent is canceled—whichever happens first. Descendant contexts observe the same upstream cancellation, so an entire request tree can stop coherently.

Authority points downward. Functions receiving a Context can observe Done and Err, but the interface has no Cancel method. The creator retains the CancelFunc, preventing a low-level database helper from canceling unrelated sibling work through the parent. Calling a CancelFunc more than once is safe; after the first call, later calls have no additional effect.

The CancelFunc also releases implementation resources and removes the child from its parent's tracking, so call it on every control-flow path. `go vet` can detect many lost-cancel mistakes. For a timeout, defer cancel immediately after successful creation even though the timer could eventually expire.

Values are the smallest part of Context and should contain request-scoped information that crosses process or API boundaries, not optional function parameters or mutable application state. Use unexported typed keys and accessors. The same Context may be read by several goroutines, but any value stored in it must itself be safe for concurrent use.

A raw done channel remains useful when one component owns one group of goroutines and no standard deadline or cause needs to propagate. Do not wrap that local convenience into a competing custom Context type. At public boundaries, accepting the standard Context lets databases, HTTP clients, and downstream services share one cancellation lifecycle.

sections.title: Choose the cancellation boundary
sections.content:
| Requirement | Custom done channel | `context.Context` |
|---|---|---|
| One local stop broadcast | Clear fit | Works but may be unnecessary |
| Parent-to-child propagation | Manual wiring | Built in |
| Deadline and error reason | Separate design | Built in |
| Standard library/API integration | Limited | Expected |
| Cancellation owner | Channel closer | Holder of CancelFunc |
